World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: More than 3 million people over 65 to pay more for private health
World.content:
More than 3 million Australians aged over 65 will have to pay hundreds of dollars more for their private health insurance per year, in a move the federal government argues will re-establish fairness between generations.

In a major pre-budget speech at the National Press Club on Wednesday, Health Minister Mark Butler announced sweeping changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme and aged care.

As part of this, he revealed older Australians would no longer be given special treatment and would now have to pay the same amount for health insurance as younger Australians.

"I understand this won't be a welcome decision for many, but it's the right thing to do," he said.

Mr Butler said the current policy was "not fair between generations" and not the best use of taxpayer money, with the decision set to save the government $3 billion over four years, which will be spent on aged care elsewhere.

The government said about 3.2 million older people would now have to pay, on average, between $226 and $255 more a year, with 44,000 older Australians expected to ditch their private health insurance as a result.

Private Healthcare Australia (PHA) chief executive Rachel David said the decision would disappoint older Australians, but she was somewhat subdued in her criticism, acknowledging it would mostly affect wealthier people who were unlikely to stop their cover.

"It will hurt consumers, impact the viability of private hospitals, and limit health funds' ability to deliver better patient experiences," Dr David said.

"[But] health funds recognise this group receives significant benefits that could be better targeted elsewhere.

"PHA has previously recommended reducing the rebate for this cohort and redistributing it to lower-income Australians who rely on private health insurance."

The difference in rebates between generations dates back to 2004 when then-prime minister John Howard made the change while Mr Butler said "government coffers [were] reaping the benefits of the China boom".

"In 2026, it's a policy that's harder to defend," he added.

Government to pay for showers for at-home aged care recipients The decision to scrap the plan to charge $50/hour for showers was made after months of sustained criticism, including warnings that people were forgoing other care to afford showers.

The policy shift came alongside Mr Butler announcing the government would spend $1 billion to fully cover the cost of showering assistance for someone on an aged care Support at Home package.

Only six months ago, the government introduced a co-payment for package recipients, but its decision to include showering and continence care as part of that proved highly controversial, with some calling it a "human rights" issue because it was costing some people $50 out-of-pocket per hour.

Elsewhere in aged care, insufficient beds across the country has had major flow-on effects to bed block in hospitals, with states demanding the federal government do more to help.

To assist, Mr Butler announced that from 2029, an extra 5,000 beds per year would be built.

More than $200 million has also been committed to establishing 20 additional dementia care units and an expanded support program to help people transition from hospital to nursing homes.

World.title: Family pays tribute after teen drowns in Kimberley accident
World.content:
The family of a 15-year-old boy who died after drowning at a remote location in Western Australia's north say they are "heartbroken by the tragic loss".

Jack Avenell died during an accident along the Kimberley coastline on April 16.

Emergency services received reports he had been recovered from the Prince Regent River just after 3pm on Thursday.

A WA Police spokesperson confirmed the teenager died at the scene.

On Wednesday, Jack's father released a statement speaking on behalf of the family.

'Impossible to comprehend'

Chad Avenell said the loss was hard to comprehend.

“We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of our beloved boy, Jack," he said.

" He was bright, energetic, and kind – a devoted son, brother, and friend who brought immeasurable joy to all our lives. "

Mr Avenell thanked crew members, emergency responders and "all those who did everything they could for Jack".

"We also know this loss is deeply felt across our community," he said.

"It is impossible to comprehend that he is gone … Jack lived a life full of adventure and embraced every moment with enthusiasm and courage."

A 'tragic accident'

At the time of the incident, Jack was a passenger on one of True North Adventure Cruises' vessels, which his father owns.

In a statement, a True North spokesperson said a "tragic accident" occurred during the excursion, resulting in Jack's death.



“We are grateful for the efforts of the crew, emergency services, and those present in responding to the accident," they said.

“Our focus is now on supporting the family, whose loss is immeasurable.”

Jack's family have asked for privacy as they continue to come to terms with their loss.

World.title: Ampol has received $25m to produce renewable diesel, but will it boost supply?
World.content:
The Queensland government has given $25 million to Ampol so it can produce renewable diesel in a bid to boost domestic fuel supplies.

The first stage of the project will be ready by 2028 and deliver up to 20 million litres of diesel every year at the Lytton oil refinery on Brisbane's bayside.

But the government said production could reach 750 million litres per year by the early 2030s under stage two of the development.

What is renewable diesel?

Renewable diesel is made using renewable feedstocks including animal fats (tallow) and canola oil.

Adjunct Professor Richard Brown from the Queensland University of Technology noted there was no strict definition for renewable diesel.

"I think given that we are in Queensland we have waste cooking oil," he said.

"We have quite a big agricultural industry here where there is a potential to get other waste material to make a type of biocrude."

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie described renewable diesel as "chemically exactly the same" as regular diesel.

"When the animal fats, tallow and so forth, go through and mix with diesel you produce more litres at the end of the process," he said.

Renewable diesel can be put in tractors, utes and diesel vehicles. (ABC News: Peter Garnish)

Can I use renewable diesel in my car?

Mr Bleijie said renewable diesel produced at the Lytton refinery could be used in "conventional" diesel cars and trucks.

"This is not like an ethanol 10 per cent where you go to a bowser and you know which is the ethanol," he said.

"This chemical compound of renewable diesel is exactly the same chemical compound of normal diesel."

Loading...

Professor Brown also suggested renewable diesel could be used in diesel-powered cars and vehicles.

"You can put it in the tractor on the farm, you can put it in the ute, you can put it in your diesel vehicle, and no-one will know the difference," he said.

Can Australia grow its own jet fuel? Australia exports billions of dollars worth of canola seed to make sustainable jet fuel that is sold back to us. This is what it will take to make it here.

"The chemical makeup of the renewable diesel that is talked about in that announcement is pretty much identical to the chemical makeup of many of the components in petrol, diesel, and aviation fuel," he said.

"The ratios of the chemicals may be a little bit different, but it's completely compatible with diesel.

"You could use 100 per cent of the renewable diesel, or you could dilute it with 10 per cent, 20 per cent, 50 per cent — whatever you wanted to do with actual diesel."

How much renewable diesel will be produced at Lytton?

Stage one of the project at the Ampol refinery would deliver up to 20 million litres of renewable diesel every year.

The government has suggested this would pave the way for stage two of the project, which would generate up to 750 million litres of renewable diesel and aviation fuel per annum.

Stage one is expected to be up and running by 2028, while stage two is scheduled to be operational by the early 2030s, according to the government.

David Crisafulli announced the $25 million investment at Ampol's Lytton refinery on Wednesday morning. (AAP: Darren England)

Premier David Crisafulli acknowledged the initial 20 million litres of diesel was not a substantial amount of fuel.

"There's no silver bullet, but we've got to pull every lever we can," he said.

" If us investing in this can ensure a trickle becomes a flood in the years to come, that's the long-term vision that people need. "

What will the $25 million go towards?

The government is giving Ampol $25 million under its Sovereign Industry Development Fund to get the project off the ground.

It has also declared the initiative a "prescribed project" which ensures it is subject to a streamlined approval process with the coordinator-general.

Construction is expected to create 46 jobs.

A secondary tank containment system and a system upgrade to process feedstock will be delivered as part of the project.

World.title: Case dropped against actor accused of 'breaking the girl code'
World.content:
Victorian prosecutors have abandoned an assault case against an Australian actor, who was accused of grabbing a woman's breast and twisting it during a scuffle at Parliament House.

The woman, a parliamentary worker, accused former Offspring actor Alicia Gardiner of breaking "the girl code" during the tussle on May 7, 2024.

Gardiner was part of a pro-Palestine group that yelled slogans and held up banners during a speech by then-treasurer Tim Pallas.

The group was evicted from the public gallery and taken to the exit of the Spring Street building.

While being kicked out, Gardiner was alleged to have bumped a female worker into a doorframe and grabbed at her chest.

The worker today told the Melbourne Magistrates' Court she felt a "sharp pain".

"She broke the girl code and twisted my breast — you don't do that," the worker said of Gardiner.

" I was really scared … and I was really angry. "

The alleged breast-grabbing incident was not captured on camera, the court heard.

Alicia Gardiner and Asher Keddie in a scene from Offspring in 2010. (Supplied: IMDb)

Another parliamentary worker, Glen Putland, said he saw Gardiner grappling with his colleague.

Gardiner contested the allegations and was set to give evidence on Wednesday afternoon.

At that stage, Magistrate Malcolm Thomas said it was possible to conclude a deliberate grab of the breast had occurred, based on the evidence.

However, an hour later, after a break, prosecutors announced they would drop the assault charge.

No explanation was given about why the case was being abandoned midway through the contested hearing.

Gardiner, who sat in the court gallery, held back tears upon learning the news.

The actor pleaded guilty to refusing to leave the parliamentary precinct and was fined $500 without conviction.

Defence barrister Angeline Centrone said her client was a 50-year-old mother of two, who had no previous criminal history.

She said Gardiner had glowing references that spoke to her "great integrity", generosity and volunteer work.

Alicia Gardiner read a short statement to the media outside court. (AAP: Con Chronis)

Outside court, Gardiner read a short statement, saying she had denied the assault allegations since being charged two years ago.

"I pled guilty today to the charge of failure to leave the parliamentary precinct," she said.

"I was there to give voice to something important, and I will continue to speak up for what I believe in."

She refused to answer questions from reporters before walking off with supporters.

Gardiner has appeared on Australian stage productions and TV shows for three decades, most notably as Kim Akerholt in Offspring. Her credits include roles on Deadloch, Kath and Kim, and Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries.

World.title: New $30.5m funding package to help repair NT roads damaged by flooding
World.content:
Ten major remote roads damaged by flooding in the Northern Territory will be repaired using funding from a $30.5 million package announced by the NT government on Wednesday.

Major flooding has impacted dozens of territory communities this wet season, damaging roads and leaving them inaccessible, and leading to hundreds of residents having to be evacuated by air.

The new repair package is in addition to a $100 million flood recovery fund announced by NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro in March.

NT's damaged roads drive up costs Workers in road-reliant industries are calling on the federal government to provide urgent funding to repair roads in the NT after severe damage from back-to-back floods.

Of the $30.5 million funding, $16 million will be spent on roads in the Big Rivers region.

They include the Roper Highway, Central Arnhem Highway, the Carpentaria Highway and Bing Bong Road.

Across the Top End, $8 million will go to repairs along Cox Penisula Road, Daly River Road, Wooliana Road and Port Keats Road.

In the Barkly region, Murray Downs Road, Elkedra Propacc Road and Kurundi Road will share $6.5 million.

Mrs Finocchiaro said sections of some roads had been completely destroyed by the flooding.

Lia Finocchiaro says the new funding is aimed at getting roads back to the condition they were in before the floods. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"We've had the most incredibly damaging and destructive wet season, starting right back in November," she said.

"Some of [the roads] don't even resemble road[s] anymore, so we've brought forward this $30 million package on top of the $100 million flood recovery [fund].

"I want that $100 million to be [used to] build back better and stronger and more resilient.

" This $30 million is just to get it back to what it was. "

The announcement comes as some Palumpa residents are expected to return to their community on Wednesday.

The community of Palumpa was flooded early last month, leading to all residents being evacuated. (Facebook: Steve Edgington)

Hundreds of people from Palumpa and Daly River/Nauiyu were evacuated to Darwin due to flooding in early March, and have been staying in evacuation centres ever since.

Most recently, they have been staying at an emergency accommodation facility in Batchelor, a small town about an hour south of Darwin.

Flood money starts to flow

Mrs Finocchiaro said the NT government had also started rolling out money from its $100 million flood recovery fund.

She said $12.5 million would go towards "flood levy and flood mitigation works in and around Katherine".

"The remaining $80 odd [million], we're now working with the Commonwealth around that," she said.

"There's significant federal programs where we can go 50:50 in some cases and so we've got to do the work around the design and the costing.

"But there's clearly some things right across the territory, and I've been really clear from the start, I want all parts of the territory to see some of that $100 million, because it wasn't just Darwin that got impacted."

World.title: Vandalised war memorial soldier repaired in time for Anzac Day
World.content:
With just days to spare, a rural town's memorial marble soldier stands ready for Anzac Day services, after repairs to a vandalised rifle.

Standing guard outside the historic Dorrigo Hotel in the NSW Mid North Coast hinterland, the 104-year-old war memorial was desecrated by vandals a week before the last Anzac Day, casting a pall over services.

Although the stone soldier has never left Dorrigo, he has been through the wars of multiple vandalism attacks and a car crash.

Laurieton stonemason Matt Bath stepped in to do the latest repairs which included repairing the soldier's damaged rifle.

He said he 'dropped everything' to carve a piece of Carrara marble when it arrived from Italy, "luckily" finishing and installing it six days before Anzac Day.

"It does mean a lot to me, and it was a real privilege to be involved," Mr Bath said.

"My grandfather fought in the Second World War and my older brother is recently retired from the army after he served for almost 20 years, over in Afghanistan, Iraq and other places."

Stonemason-carver Matt Bath chisels fine rifle details into Italian Carrara marble. (Supplied: Matt Bath)

Mr Bath's commitment to the project led him to make improvements on the previously restored rifle, as he noticed more refined details could be incorporated to the design.

"I went down to our local Laurieton RSL Club and noticed they had a couple of Lee-Enfield rifles on display," he said.

"I introduced myself and explained what I was doing and they were happy for me to take some photos.

" I could use those ceremonial rifles to take much more detailed pictures and measurements of some of the finer details, like the sight and bolt mechanisms. "

The marble rifle was modelled on the Lee-Enfield Australian infantry service weapons at Laurieton RSL Club. (Supplied: Matt Bath)

Dorrigo's military history

Dorrigo is also the hometown of Trooper Mark Donaldson, who received the Victoria Cross for his actions during an ambush in Afghanistan.

Dorrigo RSL Club president Jim McLeod said the sub-branch is relieved the monument has been repaired and cleaned in time for their dawn service and march on Saturday.

Dorrigo RSL Club president Jim McLeod is happy the war memorial soldier has his rifle back for Anzac Day. (Supplied: Tess McLeod)

"It does rather glow in the morning sun, we're really happy with the result," Mr McLeod said.

"I believe the soldier himself was actually carved in Italy and it looks like the hat on top is not quite the Australian fur felt, it's more like an Austrian type military hat, but it suits the purpose pretty well."

The rifle was damaged when a 28-year-old man climbed the war memorial, breaking off the rifle barrel, which a 24-year-old woman then put in her underwear, making lewd movements during a drinking session at the nearby hotel.

After a public appeal, a Central West NSW couple surrendered to police, pleading guilty to wilful damage of a war memorial and an offensive act on a war memorial.

Missing the barrel, the marble soldier at Dorrigo holds a broken rifle after the vandalism. (Supplied: Phillip Corlis)

Both fined by the court, the man was also ordered to pay $25,000 towards repairs.

"This is actually his third rifle, the original one was broken in a similar act of vandalism and was later found out at the tip," Mr McLeod said.

"We're going to gather all of the bits of all the broken rifles and the pieces will appear in a display cabinet at the RSL club some time in the future."

" He has his own battle scars, if you like. "

Monument owner Bellingen Shire Council, submitted an insurance claim for repairs, sourced the marble and called for tenders to repair the statue.

"This memorial holds deep meaning for the Dorrigo community," Bellingen mayor Steve Allan said.

"Places like this are where our community comes together to reflect, remember and honour those who have served, and we're proud to see it restored with care and respect."

Workmen replace the restored marble soldier in 2021, after it was damaged in a road crash. (ABC News: Claudia Jambor)

The latest repairs followed a major restoration project five years ago, after both the granite plinth and soldier were knocked down by a motorist in 2020.

"The only damage done then was to the rear brim of his hat and he managed to hang onto his rifle very well indeed and it survived intact," Mr McLeod said.

Dorrigo War Memorial, toppled nearly intact onto a car which crashed at the intersection in 2020. (Supplied: Peter Mortimore)

Since the vandalism last year, the Minns Labor government has introduced tougher penalties for intentional or reckless damage of war memorials, which can now lead to up to seven years in prison.

World.title: Netball Australia CEO steps down as sport prepares for new era
World.content:
Stacey West will step down as chief executive officer of Netball Australia at the end of this week, ending a two-and-a-half-year tenure that has reshaped the sport in this country.

West, who has spent 16 years with Netball Australia, took over as CEO in December of 2023, after predecessor Kelly Ryan stepped down following a bitter pay dispute with players.

How free is netball's new TV deal? Uncertainties over the details of Netball Australia's broadcast agreement with Nine left fans hesitant to celebrate. Now we reveal how many games will actually be seen on free-to-air TV.

Her resignation comes one week after Netball Australia announced a new five-year broadcast rights deal with the Nine Network, and five months after the organisation announced its 10-year plan, Made in Netball.

"This role has been a labour of love for me," West said.

"My commitment to the sport, our people and our athletes, has been a lifelong vocation and the opportunity to contribute to our growth and success has been a privilege."

Netball Australia will begin its new free-to-air TV deal with the Nine Network from January 1, 2027.

A minimum of two Super Netball matches per week will be shown on free-to-air television across the course of the deal.

West said she was stepping down at a time that the sport was in a strong position to grow.

Netball star calls for pay increase after new broadcast deal Diamonds and Melbourne Vixens star Jo Weston calls for a pay increase after a new free-to-air broadcast deal.

"I hand over the reins at the dawn of a new era with the sport poised for continued success," she said.

"Super Netball continues to set crowd, audience and membership records.

"Our new long-term free-to-air broadcast partnership defies market trends and is built off the wonderful product and people who make up this sport.

"We remain the number one sport for women and girls, and the love and respect in the community for both the high performance and participation aspects of our game is the backbone of our culture and dominance."

West will be replaced by Mark Falvo who will take over as interim CEO from Monday. Falvo is the CEO of Netball World Cup Sydney 2027.

"Mark Falvo has accepted responsibility for the leadership of both our entities, and he will deliver strong value to netball based on his personal expertise and deep knowledge of the Australian and global sporting landscape," Netball Australia chair Liz Ellis said in a statement.

"Stacey and Mark already work very closely to discharge their duties and responsibilities, and a positive and collaborative transition plan is already being executed."

World.title: How these households divide and conquer mealtimes
World.content:
We've spoken to precision meal preppers and passionate family cooks, but there are many other households that have found more budget-friendly and manageable meal solutions.

From share houses to a single-person apartment, this is how three households manage the cooking very differently.

A case for communal cooking

"No-one looks forward to my night of cooking because I'm the worst cook in the house," Penny Bradley says.

Penny Bradley (right) and a housemate serving dinner together. (Supplied: Penny Bradley)

The 34-year-old teacher lives with four other adults in their 30s in Naarm/Melbourne and says being involved in the cooking roster has become a non-negotiable for any potential new housemates.

"You put your name down for one night of the week and you cook for the entire household."

The dinner roster runs from Sunday to Thursday and other meals and snacks are sorted out independently, she says.

"If you're not there [for dinner] you'll get a little Tupperware container for lunch the next day."

How is shopping and cooking managed in your household? Share you tips with us. Email lifestyle@abc.net.au

As a child, Penny felt dinner with her family was always "a really special time to come together and talk about your day".

The dinner roster cultivates that feeling of belonging and community, which also means you're less likely to be out during the week, Penny says.

"You're also saving money in that way."

Saving on money — and time

As a result of their communal dinners, Penny says her once-weekly food shop is very minimal.

Breakfast and lunch are variations of toast, salad and tuna with rice, she says.

"If you can get lunch under four bucks it's so good. It's a little game I play with myself but it's getting harder these days."

But everyone is generous when cooking for each other, she says. Dinners are all vegetarian, which can help with costs.

"Everyone puts heaps of effort into their night of cooking. You might be in the kitchen for one and a half hours but that could be it for the week."

Penny Bradley's busy share house includes tradies, a graphic designer and someone who works in advertising. (Supplied: Penny Bradley)

From share house to solo living

Food writer and content strategist Gemma Plunkett rents an apartment in Potts Point on Gadigal land in Sydney.

She enjoys where she lives, but it's expensive.

The 30-year-old grew up in the country and has loved living in an area where she can easily walk to everything she needs.

She spent her first six years "down the road" in a share house, but then moved into in her own apartment two years ago.

Gemma Plunkett says she enjoys the process of cooking at the end of the day. (Supplied: Nikki To)

Living alone has made her more aware of the leftovers she generates, and she's found neighbours, the butcher and others to be "happy recipients".

"I also have a lot of friends that live in the area that I end up feeding a lot. People will just pop by for lunch or pop by for dinner and we'll eat here."

Gemma says she loves inviting people over for a meal and if you keep things simple, hosting can be less costly than eating out.

"If you've got lovely friends, then they might return the favour".

Among the most common thing Gemma cooks for herself is roast chicken.

"You have the chicken, and then you can make a stock, and you can make a soup, or you can make a curry … so I'm not sick of it."

Gemma also freezes individual portions of food such as taco mince to avoid waste and keep things varied during busy weeks.

'A really stocked pantry'

There's not a lot of space in Gemma's compact kitchen, so the linen cupboard has been transformed into the pantry.

"I'm always kind of thinking about keeping that pantry stocked. If tinned tomatoes, chickpeas, pasta or whatever are on sale I'll buy it."

Having ingredients such as Dijon mustard, sherry vinegar, Tabasco, parmesan and olive oil are the non-negotiable (and pricier) items she relies on.

"A good sherry vinegar, Dijon mustard with some olive oil can make the saddest salad a bit more interesting."

Gemma says she's lucky to be confident enough to experiment with recipes, and as a result her focus is what's seasonal and on sale when grocery shopping.

"The more I've learnt about cooking, the more cookbooks I read, the more new recipes I try, the easier it is for me to be flexible with the way that I cook."

Gemma Plunkett says her approach to cooking relies on her pantry, which was a linen cupboard in a previous life. (Supplied: Gemma Plunkett)

An ad hoc share-house approach

Tully Rigioni lives in a five-person share house in Naarm/Melbourne where housemates typically cook for themselves.

The 24-year-old is studying and moved into the house in December 2024, but she had stayed before and was already friends with her housemates.

Tully Rigoni (right) says her share house is one of the most important things in her life. (Supplied: Tully Rigoni)

They tend to share staples between them such as onions, stock cubes and sauces, she says.

Despite there being no formal routine, Tully says she does sometimes pair up with another housemate to share the cooking.

There is a give and take that happens naturally in the house, whether it's to avoid something going bad or because it looks like someone may have had a bad day, she says.

"You wouldn't eat someone's pre-made meal in a meal prep container, but then often we'll just say 'oh, I've got this, it needs to be eaten'."

"It is a nice system, and it does seem to work. I don't know if it'll be as simple in future houses."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

"Because I've started studying again, it's become a lot more challenging [to afford food]," Tully says.

"I've had to think about what I'm eating a lot more."

In her current routine, Tully says she usually cooks two big dishes a week to cover her dinners. Curry is a regular feature.

It's then yoghurt or eggs for breakfast and a packed lunch, such as a ham roll, she says.

Her aim is to "spend as little on food as possible" and consequently, she's become a fresh market shopper.

"I love going to the market and … It is so awesome to walk away and have spent like $15 on vegetables."

But what didn't work?

Tully says shopping at the market without a plan has been a mistake for her.

"I will just buy heaps because I get excited and then I just have more food waste."

She's learnt to be more realistic about what she has the time to cook — even if there are some very cheap veggies.

"I'm not going make an Ottolenghi salad on a Tuesday night," Tully says.

Tully Rigoni says housemates often share fruit and vegetables to avoid them going bad. (Supplied: Tully Rigoni )

Gemma tried a stricter approach to meal planning and prepping for herself, but it was "just a bit of a disaster".

She enjoys the flexibility of saying yes to an impromptu dinner offer elsewhere.

"If you've got five chicken breasts prepared in the fridge, it's just going to go to waste."

Having lived in several share houses, Penny says she prefers the communal approach to dinner rather than waiting for your turn in the kitchen.

In previous homes, cooking separately also meant more cooking, cleaning and food waste, she says.

Her current home functions quite seamlessly — apart from an occasional sink strainer offence — but at other houses the kitchen experiences were not as frictionless.

From food going off in the fridge, a gecko in a cereal box, to mistakenly throwing out suspicious looking (and smelling) smoked quail eggs, she's very grateful for the current harmony.

World.title: Kyle called his boss a ‘dog’ live on air, KIIS’ owner alleges
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Kyle called his boss a ‘dog’ live on air, KIIS’ owner alleges Calum Jaspan Updated April 22, 2026 — 5:14pm ,first published 10:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Kyle Sandilands branded the man who is now chief executive of his radio network a “p---y” during a broadcast last year, saying he didn’t “give a shit” because he thought the executive would soon be out of a job. Instead, ARN chief executive Michael Stephenson sacked Sandilands last month. The comments, alongside Sandilands’ threatening remarks against members of the Mad F---ing Witches activist group, and claims of systemic bullying against his co-host Jackie “O” Henderson, form part of ARN’s defence against his $85 million contract claim in the Federal Court. Kyle Sandilands and Jackie “O” Henderson are embroiled in a messy legal squabble. Michael Howard Stephenson, a former Nine sales boss, joined ARN in late 2024 as its chief operating officer (COO). By June 2025, Sandilands was insulting him live on air, according to the documents. “Because a lot of these p---ies, they show up, they think they’re in charge,” Sandilands said on June 30. “Oh, I’m the COO. Whatever that means ... No one gives a rat’s ass, dog. And anyway, that bloke will be gone in eight months’ time anyway. Do you know how many COOs I’ve been through? Thousands.”



Sandilands went on to lambast Stephenson, saying he was from the “The C-suites ... The [expletive] suite. Where do all the [expletives] work! … That’s why they’re called the C-suites.” Stephenson, who became chief executive shortly after the comments were made, had employed a number of measures to rein in Sandilands, including adding more censors to the program after ARN was rebuked by the industry watchdog. In March this year, ARN tore up Henderson’s contract after she allegedly refused to work with Sandilands because of his conduct towards her. It then scrapped his contract too, prompting both stars to sue the network separately for at least a combined $160 million. On Tuesday, ARN filed its defence to the claims, which includes a letter Henderson’s lawyers sent the station in the wake of Sandilands’ on-air tirade against her on February 20 that broke their partnership. The lawyers said that Sandilands’ “consistent and ongoing bullying” of Henderson left her “psychologically unwell, defamed and humiliated”. ARN failed in its duty of care to protect her, the lawyers alleged, and as a result, she could no longer work with him.



In its defence to Sandilands’ claim that his contract was unfairly torn up, the network claims his conduct was so poor it had to dismiss him despite his contention that he was merely playing the controversial character expected of him. And ARN alleges that Henderson rebuffed its attempts to investigate Sandilands, despite her bullying complaints, so it could no longer employ her on her existing contract when she ultimately decided she could no longer work with her co-host of 25 years. On September 10 last year, Sandilands is alleged to have said he had carried the show by himself for more than a year in remarks that were off-air but were filmed. Loading “Don’t f---ing bother coming back until you’ve got your f---ing shit together like a normal person,” Sandilands allegedly said, referring to Henderson. “I’ve been carrying the whole show for a f---ing year … I’m just left here with a limp d--- in my hand.”



After Henderson complained, the documents state that ARN’s then-chief content officer Lauren Joyce wrote to her manager Gemma O’Neill asking for further details and stating “this is a serious matter, and Jackie’s wellbeing is our priority”. The next day, O’Neill wrote back saying that the company should already have all the information it needed. Then in December, O’Neill told the company the issue was “resolved”. Additionally, the day after the February 20 episode, Henderson thanked Stephenson, ARN’s new chief executive, and content chief Kerrie Elstub for “checking in” on her. Related Article CBD Kyle and Jackie O’s boss faces heat over his fat pay packet ARN’s defence, and claims it had attempted to investigate bullying complaints, contrast with Henderson’s claim in the letter sent by her lawyers on February 26 that claimed the company had not taken the required action to act in compliance with its obligations to provide a safe place of work. Media and entertainment lawyer Shaun Miller told this masthead it was unlikely ARN would be held responsible for not investigating a matter that, according to Henderson’s manager, had been resolved.



“The conclusion you would draw from Gemma saying that it’s resolved is that there’s nothing further to investigate,” Miller said. ARN’s lawyers argue the February 20 incident was not isolated nor accidental, but part of “a persistent course of workplace bullying and harassment of Ms Henderson” that she “had complained” about. After the Kyle and Jackie O show breached a number of industry codes in October last year, the court documents note ARN directed Sandilands to not discuss a range of topics during the show, including criticism of ARN executives or staff, any topic that included ongoing legal proceedings or was being considered by media regulator ACMA or ARN shareholder News Corp. The following month, during a discussion on ACMA, and the Mad F---ing Witches activist group that had been targeting advertisers on the Kyle & Jackie O Show, Sandilands said he could “get nasty behind the scenes if I have to”. “And I don’t want to. Well, I don’t want to be burning houses down and shit like that,” he said. He also said the activist group’s conduct should be “illegal” and he would address it with his lawyers and private investigators.



Representatives for Sandilands, Henderson and ARN were contacted for comment. Both Sandilands and Henderson’s cases will be back in the Federal Court on Friday for procedural hearings. Pepito’s is a Peruvian restaurant and bar owned by cinematographer Jose Alkon. He works with head chef Sushant Khatri to bring his traditional Peruvian family recipes to a modern audience, using local produce to create a menu of snacky small plates.

The leche de tigre is the signature dish (fish ceviche, prawns and fried calamari layered with a punchy lime and chilli sauce), but you should also try perennial favourite papa a la Huancaina (potatoes with salsa criolla and a gently spicy, creamy sauce) as a side to grilled ox heart, beef tenderloin and chicken skewers.

The bar specialises in pisco, a high-proof grape brandy named Peru’s national spirit, and if you’re partial to a margarita you’ll appreciate the creamy zest of a pisco sour. There’s seating inside among the vintage movie posters, or a fairy-lit courtyard out the back.

Keep an eye on their social media – the best time to book is when there’s a live music event, like Peruvian punk rock.

World.title: Hastings eyes US$53M first-year revenue from Thai rare earths plant
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Hastings eyes US$53M first-year revenue from Thai rare earths plant Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward April 22, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The countdown to Hastings Tecnology Metals’ maiden revenue stream is officially on after the company pulled the curtain back on a proprietary flowsheet for its Kabin Buri Hydromet Plant in Thailand. The company says that the facility remains on track for first production of mixed rare earth chloride flake in the final quarter of this year, with unaudited estimates projecting a massive $US53.4 million (A$74.68M) in year-one revenue. The Kabin Buri Industrial Zone in Thailand is home to Hasting Technology Metals new Hydromet plant. Hastings’ push into Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor via the Kabin Buri hydromet plant appears a savvy strategic play, potentially delivering near-term cash flow from a globally connected industrial hub. Better still, the timing looks spot on, with that revenue stream likely to underpin the development costs of its flagship Yangibana rare earths and niobium joint venture in Western Australia. By moving downstream now, Hastings is effectively accelerating its transition from a pure-play miner to a vertically integrated producer far earlier than previously envisaged.



‘Hastings is on a clear, near-term path to first MREC production.’ Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania The numbers attached to the Thai play are eye-catching. In the first year, the plant is expected to pump out 6000 tonnes of mixed rare earth chloride (MREC) for a solid estimated pretax profit of $US21.6 million (A$30M). Under the current structure, Hastings’ 49 per cent interest would net the company $US10.6 million (A$15M) in its first year alone. However, the real growth story lands during the plant’s second year of operations. Following a planned $US3 million expansion, production is expected to double to 12,000 tonnes per annum of MREC. At the boosted rate, the plant’s annual revenue is projected to double to an eye-watering $US106.8 million (A$149M), with pretax profits climbing to a hefty $US43.8 million (A$61.25). Looking further ahead, the company is already eyeing a massive fivefold scale-up to 30,000 tonnes annually, Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania said: “With feed stock secured and a proven seven-stage process ready for commissioning, Hastings is on a clear, near-term path to first MREC production.”



The company has recently cleared the pathway to revenue generation by nailing a cornerstone two-year offtake agreement with Enuo Holdings for 5000 tonnes of African monazite concentrate annually. The high-grade African feedstock packs a punch, delivering a 54 per cent total rare earth oxide grade. The concentrate is also loaded with 20 per cent of the lucrative magnet metals powering the world, neodymium and praseodymium, rounded out by significant volumes of dysprosium and terbium. Technically, the plant uses a proven seven-stage process, involving caustic cracking and hydrochloric acid leaching to convert the monazite concentrate into premium-grade MREC. The refined product is highly sought after by global oxide separation facilities as it can be used immediately, avoiding the extra cost and time needed to dissolve it again. Operating in Thailand also provides a structural cost advantage. Hastings expects materially lower unit costs than in Western jurisdictions, thanks to cheaper electricity and reagents, as well as a deep pool of local engineering talent. For Hastings, the Kabin Buri plant appears to offer a slicker, capital-light downstream pathway for early cash flow. Kabin Buri bridges the gap, allowing the company to bypass its immediate need for a yet-to-be-built local hydromet plant in Australia to process its expected rare earth concentrate.



Once the plant is ramped up to full capacity, the company expects to have the flexibility to treat multiple third-party suppliers. This could also include concentrate from its own impressive Yangibana rare earths project in WA, if Hastings and its JV partner assess it as the preferred route for Yangibana ore. Hastings and Wyloo, its 40 per cent joint venture partner at Yangibana, sit on a 21m-tonne ore reserve grading 0.9 per cent total rare earth oxides. However, what sets it apart from its peers is a 37 per cent ratio of EV magnet rare earths of neodymium and praseodymium. The current Yangibana plan is to upgrade the ore in WA through a proposed local hydromet plant still to be built. But Wyloo chief executive Luca Giocovazzi says the new Thailand facility could emerge as a valuable strategic alternative for the joint venture. Giocovazzi said: “It represents a capital-efficient downstream pathway and a fast route to market for one of the world’s highest-grade NdPr deposits. Wyloo is working closely with Hastings and we look forward to jointly exploring the economic benefits of this processing option.” The countdown to cash flow is well and truly on for Hastings. With a savvy pivot to a capital-light model in Thailand, they appear to have turned a long-term development story into a potential near-term revenue generator. World.title: ‘Clear case of cronyism’: Former school building boss Anthony Manning found corrupt by ICAC
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWSchools ‘Clear case of cronyism’: Former school building boss Anthony Manning found corrupt by ICAC Michael McGowan April 22, 2026 — 4:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The former head of the NSW school building agency has been referred to the Director of Public Prosecutions after the state’s anti-corruption watchdog found he acted corruptly in a “clear case of cronyism”. The Independent Commission Against Corruption on Wednesday released the findings of Operation Landan, a long-running investigation into the former chief executive of School Infrastructure NSW, Anthony Manning. Former School Infrastructure NSW chief executive Anthony Manning leaving the Independent Commission Against Corruption last year. Sam Mooy The investigation, which culminated in a marathon public inquiry lasting more than seven weeks last year, examined claims that Manning awarded friends and associates lucrative contracts without disclosing conflicts of interest. The ICAC said on Wednesday it had found Manning, who held one of the most senior roles in the NSW education system, engaged in corrupt conduct, spending millions of dollars intended for school projects on consultants and contingent workers who were his friends and associates.



Two of those associates – Martin Berry and another former School Infrastructure employee, Wendy O’Brien – were also found to have engaged in corrupt conduct relating to Manning’s actions. The ICAC said it was “of the opinion that consideration should be given to obtaining the advice of the Director of Public Prosecutions” in relation to all three. Although the commission did not find that Manning obtained a personal financial benefit, his conduct was “a clear case of cronyism”, ICAC Commissioner Paul Lakatos SC said. “Public money that had been put aside to build and improve schools for NSW children was instead spent on jobs for friends and associates of the chief executive.” The ICAC investigation came after Manning’s abrupt departure from the role in February 2024. The Sydney Morning Herald first reported his referral to the watchdog, as well as concerns over an axed $40 million school building contract awarded by the agency.



At the heart of the ICAC inquiry were four contractors, and their relationship with the former school building boss; Berry, Stuart Suthern-Brunt, Michael Palassis and Kathy Jones. There were no findings against Suthern-Brunt, Palassis or Jones. In total, the four contractors and their associated companies earned some $18 million from School Infrastructure during Manning’s time at the agency. All four had connections to Manning outside of School Infrastructure. All four had personal and professional relationships with him. Related Article ICAC A new boss, his buddies and a $2.6 billion cash splash: Inside the ICAC probe into School Infrastructure Manning had known Berry since 2006 and organised his buck’s party. He took spin and yoga classes with Suthern-Brunt, and once described Jones as his “communications fairy godmother”. In 2017, he and Palassis were part of a group trying to develop a “cancer wellness” hospital in China close to the time his company, Paxon, were bidding along with PwC to win a tender with the agency.



It also heard evidence large sums of money flowed to associates of Manning’s, including members of his “Tom, Dick and Harry Breakfast Club” and “Cycling” and “Beer and Curry” groups. Manning was the first chief executive of School Infrastructure NSW, a government agency set up by the then Coalition government in 2017 to deliver and maintain public schools. The ICAC heard evidence that when the agency was established, the government held doubts over the Education Department’s ability to deliver on an ambitious school building agenda. Running through the inquiry was a sense that Manning believed he had been brought in to shake things up.



Rob Stokes, who was education minister when the agency was set up but was not accused of any wrongdoing, described a feeling of “exasperation” with the department over issues such as a new high-rise school, Arthur Phillip in Parramatta, which was plagued by cost blow-outs and delays. It led to a culture where consultants within the agency earned significant salaries. Murat Dizdar, the current education secretary, gave evidence 26 people were on salaries of more than $500,000 a year when he took over in 2023, and the ICAC heard that some 1400 consultants were paid $344 million over seven years. Also key to the investigation was whether Manning and others engaged in “reprisal action” against staff who raised concerns. Andrea Patrick, a senior procurement officer at the department who was fired by Manning, alleged that at a meeting in 2017 he “made a comment along the lines of ‘I don’t need you or services or policies’.” She claimed Manning told her he had a “direct line” to ministers and said words to the effect of “if I need to do things different, I just pick up the phone to them, and they’ll sort it”.



She, along with others, was later sacked. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ASX slumps on war uncertainty, Cochlear tanks; BHP gains on China breakthrough
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slumps on war uncertainty, Cochlear tanks; BHP gains on China breakthrough Staff writers Updated April 22, 2026 — 4:48pm ,first published April 22, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket slumped on Wednesday amid lingering uncertainty about the duration of the Middle East war after plans for a fresh round of talks between the US and Iran fell apart overnight, although President Donald Trump agreed to extend a ceasefire. Cochlear lost more than a third of its market value after it issued a profit warning, saying consumer confidence had hit demand for its hearing aids. BHP shares gained after the mining giant finalised a supply deal with China’s state-backed iron ore buyer, ending a tense, months-long standoff. China’s state-backed buyer has buried the hatchet with BHP. Dave Tacon The S&P/ASX 200 slid 105.80 points, or 1.2 per cent, to 8843.60, with healthcare and financial stocks leading its losses. The Australian dollar was 0.3 per cent higher at US71.71¢ at 4.42pm AEST. The ASX treaded water on Tuesday as investors were holding out for any progress on peace talks. Trump announced on Wednesday morning he was extending a ceasefire with Iran indefinitely a day before it was set to expire. The US would hold off on fresh attacks on mediating nation Pakistan’s request, but would maintain its blockade of the key Strait of Hormuz, which remains at a virtual standstill.



Without the blockade, “there can never be a Deal with Iran, unless we blow up the rest of their Country, their leaders included!“, the US president said in a social media post. Vice President JD Vance had been due to travel to Islamabad to resume talks with Iran, but representatives from Tehran refused to attend, citing what they said were unreasonable US demands. Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency said there is currently no prospect of Iran participating in negotiations. Related Article Live

Middle East at war US-Iran war live updates: IRGC gunboat fires on ship in Hormuz; Trump says US will extend ceasefire, blockade to continue “Both the US and Iran may be trying to shore up leverage and playing a game of who blinks first,” said Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp strategist Christopher Wong. “Whatever the outcome, the suspense in the interim may see risk appetite being curtailed.” Cochlear was the biggest loser of the trading session on the ASX, with its shares tanking 40.7 per cent after the company shaved its profit forecast for the year by up to a third, citing uncertainty in the Middle East, the rising Aussie dollar and disappointing demand in its main markets, where consumer confidence was waning and addressing hearing loss was still being “treated as a discretionary intervention”. Full-year profit would come in at between $290 million and $330 million, down from a previous forecast of $435 million to $460 million, it warned.



Financial stocks also weighed heavily on the market, with all big four banks losing between 2.1 per cent (Westpac) and 2.5 per cent (CBA), and “Millionaires’ Factory” Macquarie Group slumping 3.8 per cent. Bank of Queensland shares plunged 9.1 per cent after the regional bank reported cash earnings fell 4 per in its first half, to $176 million. Defying the market’s sea of red, BHP shares climbed 1.2 per cent. The world’s biggest miner has concluded iron ore sales contract negotiations with China Mineral Resources Group, it said in an operational update. Terms, including pricing mechanisms and contract duration, weren’t disclosed. Related Article Opinion

Iron ore BHP has won the battle, but China’s $93b iron ore flex will continue Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The resolution allows BHP renewed access to its largest market after around seven months of disruption. In September, CMRG escalated a pricing dispute with the miner by urging steel mills to halt purchases of its Jimblebar Fines blend, a ban that was later extended to other BHP products over months of a breakdown in commercial negotiations. Iron ore rival Fortescue was up 0.1 per cent, and Rio Tinto slipped 0.5 per cent. Meanwhile, gold miners Northern Star Resources (down 3.6 per cent), Evolution Mining (down 2.9 per cent) and Newmont (down 1.7 per cent) struggled even as gold held some ground after a two-day decline, rising as much as 1.1 per ent to $US4,770 an ounce, after falling more than 2 per cent in the previous session.



Energy stocks wiped out early gains in the afternoon after Iran said that despite Trump’s pledge, it received “some sign” that the US was willing to end its blockade, opening the path for talks between the nations. Brent declined as much as 2 per cent to near $US97 a barrel after adding almost 9 per cent in the previous two sessions, while West Texas Intermediate was around $US88. Local oil and gas giant Woodside lost 1.4 per cent, while Santos closed unchanged. Refiner Ampol held on to its 3.8 per cent, gain, while Viva Energy shed 0.4 per cent. Consumer staples benefited as investors shifted to more defensive industries amid the war jitters, with Woolworths up 0.9 per cent and Coles finishing the day 0.4 per cent higher. Treasury Wine Estates was the biggest winner, rallying 16.5 per cent after reaffirming its profit forecast for the year, citing improved depletions - a key sales metric in the wine industry - in China and the US and announcing a new, regional business structure to more effectively run its business. In New York overnight, Wall Street and oil prices flip-flopped as the Middle East uncertainty hovered over markets. Uncertainty over the Middle East ceasefire is hovering over markets. Bloomberg



The S&P 500 erased an early rise to fall 0.6 per cent, the Dow Jones dropped 293 points, or 0.6 per cent, after erasing an earlier gain of 400 points, while the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.6 per cent. The US stock market remains near its most recent record, indicating optimism still remains in financial markets that the United States and Iran will avoid a worst-case scenario for the economy. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve No ‘sock puppet’? What to expect from Trump’s pick for the Fed chair Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “It’s become clichéd to say that the economic hit will depend on the duration of the Middle East conflict, but that cliché does ring true,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Much of the tension in financial markets has focused on what will happen to the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway off Iran’s coast that oil tankers use to exit the Persian Gulf. A long-term closure would keep crude oil pent up in the gulf and away from customers worldwide.



Helping to limit Wall Street’s losses were UnitedHealth Group and other big companies that reported bigger profits for the latest quarter than analysts expected. UnitedHealth jumped 7 per cent after also raising its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. That’s big because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, and it’s a double-plus when companies not only top earnings estimates but also forecast better growth ahead. Amazon added 0.7 per cent after Anthropic said it signed a new agreement and is committing more than $US100 billion ($140 billion) over the next 10 years to AWS technologies to train and run its Claude chatbot. Kevin Warsh during his testimony before the Senate Banking Committee. Bloomberg But they were all nevertheless overshadowed by a 2.5 per cent drop for Apple, which was the day’s heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It fell in its first trading session after Tim Cook said he’ll step down as CEO on September 1 and become the iPhone maker’s executive chairman.



Cook is handing control over to John Ternus, a company veteran who rose through Apple’s hardware engineering ranks. In the bond market, Treasury yields rose after a report on Tuesday morning showed that US retailers made more money in March, the first full month of the war, than analysts expected. Growth was even relatively stable for retail sales when not including those from petrol stations. The yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 4.31 per cent from 4.26 per cent late Monday, and the gains accelerated late in the day with oil prices. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Kyle Sandilands and Jackie “O” Henderson are embroiled in a messy legal squabble. Michael Howard Stephenson, a former Nine sales boss, joined ARN in late 2024 as its chief operating officer (COO). By June 2025, Sandilands was insulting him live on air, according to the documents. “Because a lot of these p---ies, they show up, they think they’re in charge,” Sandilands said on June 30. “Oh, I’m the COO. Whatever that means ... No one gives a rat’s ass, dog. And anyway, that bloke will be gone in eight months’ time anyway. Do you know how many COOs I’ve been through? Thousands.”



Sandilands went on to lambast Stephenson, saying he was from the “The C-suites ... The [expletive] suite. Where do all the [expletives] work! … That’s why they’re called the C-suites.” Stephenson, who became chief executive shortly after the comments were made, had employed a number of measures to rein in Sandilands, including adding more censors to the program after ARN was rebuked by the industry watchdog. In March this year, ARN tore up Henderson’s contract after she allegedly refused to work with Sandilands because of his conduct towards her. It then scrapped his contract too, prompting both stars to sue the network separately for at least a combined $160 million. On Tuesday, ARN filed its defence to the claims, which includes a letter Henderson’s lawyers sent the station in the wake of Sandilands’ on-air tirade against her on February 20 that broke their partnership. The lawyers said that Sandilands’ “consistent and ongoing bullying” of Henderson left her “psychologically unwell, defamed and humiliated”. ARN failed in its duty of care to protect her, the lawyers alleged, and as a result, she could no longer work with him.



In its defence to Sandilands’ claim that his contract was unfairly torn up, the network claims his conduct was so poor it had to dismiss him despite his contention that he was merely playing the controversial character expected of him. And ARN alleges that Henderson rebuffed its attempts to investigate Sandilands, despite her bullying complaints, so it could no longer employ her on her existing contract when she ultimately decided she could no longer work with her co-host of 25 years. On September 10 last year, Sandilands is alleged to have said he had carried the show by himself for more than a year in remarks that were off-air but were filmed. Loading “Don’t f---ing bother coming back until you’ve got your f---ing shit together like a normal person,” Sandilands allegedly said, referring to Henderson. “I’ve been carrying the whole show for a f---ing year … I’m just left here with a limp d--- in my hand.”



After Henderson complained, the documents state that ARN’s then-chief content officer Lauren Joyce wrote to her manager Gemma O’Neill asking for further details and stating “this is a serious matter, and Jackie’s wellbeing is our priority”. The next day, O’Neill wrote back saying that the company should already have all the information it needed. Then in December, O’Neill told the company the issue was “resolved”. Additionally, the day after the February 20 episode, Henderson thanked Stephenson, ARN’s new chief executive, and content chief Kerrie Elstub for “checking in” on her. Related Article CBD Kyle and Jackie O’s boss faces heat over his fat pay packet ARN’s defence, and claims it had attempted to investigate bullying complaints, contrast with Henderson’s claim in the letter sent by her lawyers on February 26 that claimed the company had not taken the required action to act in compliance with its obligations to provide a safe place of work. Media and entertainment lawyer Shaun Miller told this masthead it was unlikely ARN would be held responsible for not investigating a matter that, according to Henderson’s manager, had been resolved.



“The conclusion you would draw from Gemma saying that it’s resolved is that there’s nothing further to investigate,” Miller said. ARN’s lawyers argue the February 20 incident was not isolated nor accidental, but part of “a persistent course of workplace bullying and harassment of Ms Henderson” that she “had complained” about. After the Kyle and Jackie O show breached a number of industry codes in October last year, the court documents note ARN directed Sandilands to not discuss a range of topics during the show, including criticism of ARN executives or staff, any topic that included ongoing legal proceedings or was being considered by media regulator ACMA or ARN shareholder News Corp. The following month, during a discussion on ACMA, and the Mad F---ing Witches activist group that had been targeting advertisers on the Kyle & Jackie O Show, Sandilands said he could “get nasty behind the scenes if I have to”. “And I don’t want to. Well, I don’t want to be burning houses down and shit like that,” he said. He also said the activist group’s conduct should be “illegal” and he would address it with his lawyers and private investigators.



Representatives for Sandilands, Henderson and ARN were contacted for comment. Both Sandilands and Henderson’s cases will be back in the Federal Court on Friday for procedural hearings. Pepito’s is a Peruvian restaurant and bar owned by cinematographer Jose Alkon. He works with head chef Sushant Khatri to bring his traditional Peruvian family recipes to a modern audience, using local produce to create a menu of snacky small plates.

The leche de tigre is the signature dish (fish ceviche, prawns and fried calamari layered with a punchy lime and chilli sauce), but you should also try perennial favourite papa a la Huancaina (potatoes with salsa criolla and a gently spicy, creamy sauce) as a side to grilled ox heart, beef tenderloin and chicken skewers.

The bar specialises in pisco, a high-proof grape brandy named Peru’s national spirit, and if you’re partial to a margarita you’ll appreciate the creamy zest of a pisco sour. There’s seating inside among the vintage movie posters, or a fairy-lit courtyard out the back.

Keep an eye on their social media – the best time to book is when there’s a live music event, like Peruvian punk rock.

World.title: Hastings eyes US$53M first-year revenue from Thai rare earths plant
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Hastings eyes US$53M first-year revenue from Thai rare earths plant Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward April 22, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The countdown to Hastings Tecnology Metals’ maiden revenue stream is officially on after the company pulled the curtain back on a proprietary flowsheet for its Kabin Buri Hydromet Plant in Thailand. The company says that the facility remains on track for first production of mixed rare earth chloride flake in the final quarter of this year, with unaudited estimates projecting a massive $US53.4 million (A$74.68M) in year-one revenue. The Kabin Buri Industrial Zone in Thailand is home to Hasting Technology Metals new Hydromet plant. Hastings’ push into Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor via the Kabin Buri hydromet plant appears a savvy strategic play, potentially delivering near-term cash flow from a globally connected industrial hub. Better still, the timing looks spot on, with that revenue stream likely to underpin the development costs of its flagship Yangibana rare earths and niobium joint venture in Western Australia. By moving downstream now, Hastings is effectively accelerating its transition from a pure-play miner to a vertically integrated producer far earlier than previously envisaged.



‘Hastings is on a clear, near-term path to first MREC production.’ Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania The numbers attached to the Thai play are eye-catching. In the first year, the plant is expected to pump out 6000 tonnes of mixed rare earth chloride (MREC) for a solid estimated pretax profit of $US21.6 million (A$30M). Under the current structure, Hastings’ 49 per cent interest would net the company $US10.6 million (A$15M) in its first year alone. However, the real growth story lands during the plant’s second year of operations. Following a planned $US3 million expansion, production is expected to double to 12,000 tonnes per annum of MREC. At the boosted rate, the plant’s annual revenue is projected to double to an eye-watering $US106.8 million (A$149M), with pretax profits climbing to a hefty $US43.8 million (A$61.25). Looking further ahead, the company is already eyeing a massive fivefold scale-up to 30,000 tonnes annually, Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania said: “With feed stock secured and a proven seven-stage process ready for commissioning, Hastings is on a clear, near-term path to first MREC production.”



The company has recently cleared the pathway to revenue generation by nailing a cornerstone two-year offtake agreement with Enuo Holdings for 5000 tonnes of African monazite concentrate annually. The high-grade African feedstock packs a punch, delivering a 54 per cent total rare earth oxide grade. The concentrate is also loaded with 20 per cent of the lucrative magnet metals powering the world, neodymium and praseodymium, rounded out by significant volumes of dysprosium and terbium. Technically, the plant uses a proven seven-stage process, involving caustic cracking and hydrochloric acid leaching to convert the monazite concentrate into premium-grade MREC. The refined product is highly sought after by global oxide separation facilities as it can be used immediately, avoiding the extra cost and time needed to dissolve it again. Operating in Thailand also provides a structural cost advantage. Hastings expects materially lower unit costs than in Western jurisdictions, thanks to cheaper electricity and reagents, as well as a deep pool of local engineering talent. For Hastings, the Kabin Buri plant appears to offer a slicker, capital-light downstream pathway for early cash flow. Kabin Buri bridges the gap, allowing the company to bypass its immediate need for a yet-to-be-built local hydromet plant in Australia to process its expected rare earth concentrate.



Once the plant is ramped up to full capacity, the company expects to have the flexibility to treat multiple third-party suppliers. This could also include concentrate from its own impressive Yangibana rare earths project in WA, if Hastings and its JV partner assess it as the preferred route for Yangibana ore. Hastings and Wyloo, its 40 per cent joint venture partner at Yangibana, sit on a 21m-tonne ore reserve grading 0.9 per cent total rare earth oxides. However, what sets it apart from its peers is a 37 per cent ratio of EV magnet rare earths of neodymium and praseodymium. The current Yangibana plan is to upgrade the ore in WA through a proposed local hydromet plant still to be built. But Wyloo chief executive Luca Giocovazzi says the new Thailand facility could emerge as a valuable strategic alternative for the joint venture. Giocovazzi said: “It represents a capital-efficient downstream pathway and a fast route to market for one of the world’s highest-grade NdPr deposits. Wyloo is working closely with Hastings and we look forward to jointly exploring the economic benefits of this processing option.” The countdown to cash flow is well and truly on for Hastings. With a savvy pivot to a capital-light model in Thailand, they appear to have turned a long-term development story into a potential near-term revenue generator.
